contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: Stakeholder Management: The Core of the Product Owner Role
items.summary: In almost every training session, there is a product owner who has been putting off the conversation with their toughest stakeholder for three sprints already. Odds are you have one just like that. You know exactly which conversation it is and what is at stake. You just aren't having it. That’s not a failure on your part as a PO. You are doing your job just fine, but your week is consumed by stakeholders who are all screaming that their request is priority 1. Stakeholder management is still too often dismissed as a "soft skill": an afterthought squeezed somewhere between refining your product backlog and running a tight sprint planning. What Research Says About Stakeholder Management In our National Product Owner Survey ( Nationaal Product Owner Onderzoek ), Dutch product owners have consistently cited stakeholder management as both the most critical and the most challenging aspect of their profession for years. It also tops the list of what POs want to learn themselves even ahead of product vision and roadmapping. Image Beneath that lies a metric that is less frequently linked to stakeholders: one-third of a product owner's workload consists of unplanned, ad hoc work. That is more than a day and a half each week that nobody accounted for. You feel it on Friday afternoon when the user story you planned to pick up on Monday is still untouched. In my experience, a significant portion of that starts with a stakeholder who got to your desk before you reached out to theirs. Two Different Lenses Why is that conversation often so difficult? Because as a product owner, you look at the world through a product lens : you think in terms of vision, value, team performance, backlog order, and technical feasibility. But your stakeholder is looking through an entirely different lens. They look through the lens of their domain, their targets, and the pressure coming down from above. Image You look at the world through a product lens! If you expect a stakeholder to put on your product lens, you are going to "lose" the conversation. You’ll be talking past each other! Jokingly, I often say in training: Stakeholders sometimes act just like kids right before the holidays : they all believe they’ve been the best-behaved and deserve the most presents. Taking into account the total budget or the team’s capacity? That’s your job, not theirs. And if you don't push back, you simply become part of someone else's plan. True stakeholder management is not about waving your roadmap around and saying "no." Of course, those are important elements where a roadmap helps you push back. But you are a product owner, not a product dictator. It’s about building a partnership . And that only happens when you address both sides of their needs: The business need (what information, KPIs, or outcomes do they need for their role?). The personal need (what drives them as a human being in this conversation?). Not a Single "Type," but Shifting Needs It is crucial to realize that you cannot put people into a box as a single "type" of stakeholder. It is about needs , and one person can have multiple needs simultaneously or sequentially, depending on the situation or topic: Sometimes there is a need for "Power" / Status: They want to know: what's in it for me? They test you in the first few minutes. Show immediately how your product helps them achieve their goals. Sometimes there is a need for Certainty: They want to minimize risks. Take the pressure off by walking them through your iterative approach and leveraging their domain knowledge. Sometimes there is a need for "Social" / Relationship: They want to connect first. Accept that the first 20 minutes will be about the weekend; only then do you earn their goodwill. Sometimes there is a need for Order or Realization: They want structure, action, tight agendas, and zero surprises. And there is always the "undervalued" need: Genuine recognition. Every human being wants to be seen and appreciated for their contribution and responsibility. Most POs find this very challenging, because giving recognition is not something me as a Dutch person am naturally great at. How to Actually Have That Postponed Conversation (and Boost Your Effectiveness) Put yourself in your stakeholder's shoes (and lenses) What is truly important to them? What pressure are they feeling from their own constituents? Consider using an Empathy Map (see image below) to separate hard observations from your own assumptions and interpretations. Anticipate upfront which need is central What personal and business needs does this specific stakeholder have right now? Address that directly in your preparation and communication style. Determine the exact conversation you need to have It is rarely about the prioritization order between two user stories. What it’s really about is: what information do they want to receive, through which channel, at what frequency, and in what format to satisfy their needs? Set a walk-away baseline and a stretch target…

items.title: The Element nobody lists is the one that makes the others work
items.summary: From the Scrum Guide: "Each element of the framework serves a specific purpose that is essential to the overall value and results realized with Scrum." The Cambridge Dictionary defines an element as "one of the parts of something that makes it work, or a quality that makes someone or something effective." So which parts make Scrum work? Ask a team, and you'll hear the events, the three accountabilities and the three artifacts. I hear that same list in most of my classes, even PSM Advanced and PSPO Advanced, and in most teams when I start coaching them. The element almost nobody names is the theory: transparency, inspection and adaptation. Yet that's the element that makes the others effective. Inspection compares where you want to be with where you are, to find the gap. Adaptation closes that gap. And both sides have to be transparent, or the inspection compares guesses. Take a team's skills. The objective is in the Guide. "Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint." And a few lines further, "The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities from stakeholder collaboration, verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research and development, and anything else that might be required." The current state is the skills and experience the team has today. Make both visible, and the gap shows itself. Adaptation can then take many forms: training on the job, online, in person or self-paced, coaching, mentoring. That's usually the moment it clicks in a class. The pillars aren't three items on a list. They're one loop, and the events and artifacts are where it runs. In practice, the loop often goes wrong from the start. What needs to be transparent isn't. Nobody wrote down which skills the product needs, or what the team can actually do today. The inspection then shows only part of the gap, or measures it against opinions, so the adaptation picks the wrong actions. Or the right actions get agreed and are never carried out. A 2023 Scrum Alliance survey found that only about 35% of teams consistently complete their Retrospective action items. A skills gap that gets named in a Retrospective and never acted on stays exactly where it was. Try this with your team: Ask everyone to write down every element of Scrum they can name, without looking anything up. Then open the Scrum Guide and compare. Which elements did nobody write down? For each one you missed, ask: what does this element make work for us, and what isn't working because we forgot it? items.title: Free ebook: Scrum with AI
items.summary: Image Now that an AI agent can write in an afternoon what used to take a Sprint, a quick conclusion is going around: if building no longer costs much, Scrum is no longer needed. Jeff Gothelf makes the case in Product Management and AI (Sense & Respond Press, 2026). When shipping a feature takes minutes instead of months, he argues, delivery stops being an event, and processes like Agile and Scrum are no longer needed in the same way. I think he is right about what he criticises and wrong about what he concludes. That is why I wrote Scrum with AI , a short, free book about how to use Scrum to work with AI with sound judgement. Here is what it is about and what it tries to give you. The core idea: what AI does not make cheaper AI makes building cheap. It does not make it cheaper to decide what to build, to check that it works or to answer for it. Scrum exists for the second part. If you used Scrum to protect the capacity of a scarce development team, with AI you no longer need half of it. If you use it to learn fast without losing control, you need it more than ever: inspecting and adapting with evidence, in short cycles, with someone who answers for the outcome. Gothelf is right to criticise Scrum used as a ticket factory. But what he proposes instead (hypotheses, experiments, measuring how people's behaviour changes and deciding with evidence) is Scrum's empiricism done well. The book starts from there and gets concrete. What it is about: the team that builds with agents and the company that adopts AI The book has two sides. The first is the development team that already works with agents: what changes in its Sprint, its events, its Product Backlog and its Definition of Done when code arrives much faster. The second is the company that is adopting its first AI use cases and needs to prioritise them, pilot them, measure them and comply with regulation without buying licences blindly. To keep it practical, it follows one case from start to finish: GymTonic, a fictional gym with a software team that codes with agents and a business that pilots its first uses of AI. Alongside it, I share what I have learned teaching the PSM AI Essentials and PSPO AI Essentials classes, and what we have learned at ITNOVE working with agents on our own website, mistakes included. What it tries to give you Each chapter aims to leave you with a decision made about your team or your company, not just one more idea. These are the main ones: What cannot be delegated. What each person on the team decides when AI proposes almost everything, and who answers for what it produces. An agent is not a teammate: it is capacity, and the spec becomes the Product Backlog item of a hybrid team. Also, how much a team can shrink without losing judgement. Agreements that fit on one page. How people and agents reach agreement: vibe coding to explore and specs for what stays, three levels of autonomy, and what changes in the Daily Scrum and the Sprint Retrospective. A Sprint paced by the answer, not by the code. Why the Sprint does not get shorter just because building is fast, how to discover and deliver at the same time, and how to plan when effort is no longer the constraint. "Done" is not "the agent has finished". The quality contract of a team that works with AI, and what changes when the product itself has AI inside. Knowing whether AI pays off. One ladder of goals that links strategy to the Sprint, looking at the whole value stream and not just your piece, and measuring whether AI really improves anything. Adopting AI in the company with Scrum. A backlog of use cases, pilots with a stopping criterion and the move to production, with the EU AI Act, the GDPR and human oversight inside the backlog and the Definition of Done, instead of in a committee at the end. Who it is for For people who work with Scrum: Scrum Masters, Product Owners and Product Managers, Developers, project managers and technical leads. And, underneath, for anyone who has to adopt AI in their company with sound judgement and real effect. I assume you know Scrum and have already used an AI assistant. I do not assume you have worked with agents, measured whether AI improves anything for you or read the EU AI Act. If your job is adopting AI in the company, you can go straight to Part V without reading the earlier parts. How it is organised An introduction, five parts and a closing chapter: Part I. What changes and what does not: when Scrum helps and when it gets in the way, and why the bottleneck always moves. Part II. The team: people and agents: what cannot be delegated, the Scrum Master's role, agents as capacity, working agreements, team size and how a team keeps learning when AI writes the first draft. Part III. The Sprint with AI: discovering and delivering at the same time, validating before building, planning, Sprint length, the five events and the Definition of Done. Part IV. Value, measurement and more than one team: goals, value stream, measurement and coordination…

items.title: Ebook gratuito: Scrum con IA
items.summary: Image Ahora que un agente de IA escribe en una tarde lo que antes llevaba un Sprint, circula una conclusión rápida: si construir ya no cuesta, Scrum sobra. Jeff Gothelf la plantea en Product Management and AI (Sense & Respond Press, 2026). Cuando entregar una funcionalidad lleva minutos y no meses, dice, la entrega deja de ser un acontecimiento, y procesos como Agile y Scrum ya no hacen falta de la misma manera. Creo que tiene razón en lo que critica y se equivoca en lo que concluye. Por eso he escrito Scrum con IA , un libro corto y gratuito sobre cómo usar Scrum para trabajar con IA con criterio. Te cuento de qué va y qué intenta aportarte. La idea central: lo que la IA no abarata La IA abarata construir. No abarata decidir qué construir, comprobar que funciona ni responder de ello. Scrum existe para lo segundo. Si usabas Scrum para proteger la capacidad de un equipo de desarrollo escaso, con IA te sobra la mitad. Si lo usas para aprender rápido sin perder el control, te hace más falta que antes: inspeccionar y adaptar con evidencia, en ciclos cortos, con alguien que responde de lo que sale. Gothelf acierta cuando critica el Scrum usado como fábrica de tickets. Pero lo que propone como alternativa (hipótesis, experimentos, medir cómo cambia el comportamiento de la gente y decidir con evidencia) es el empirismo de Scrum bien hecho. El libro parte de ahí y baja a lo concreto. De qué va: el equipo que construye con agentes y la empresa que adopta la IA El libro tiene dos vertientes. La primera es el equipo de desarrollo que ya trabaja con agentes: qué cambia en su Sprint, en sus eventos, en su Product Backlog y en su Definición de Terminado cuando el código llega mucho más rápido. La segunda es la empresa que adopta sus primeros casos de uso de IA y necesita priorizarlos, pilotarlos, medirlos y cumplir la normativa sin comprar licencias a ciegas. Para que no se quede en teoría, sigue un caso de principio a fin: GymTonic, un gimnasio ficticio con un equipo de software que programa con agentes y un negocio que pilota sus primeros usos de la IA. Junto a él cuento lo que he aprendido impartiendo los cursos PSM AI Essentials y PSPO AI Essentials, y lo que hemos aprendido en ITNOVE trabajando con agentes en nuestra propia web, errores incluidos. Qué intenta aportarte Cada capítulo busca que termines con una decisión tomada sobre tu equipo o tu empresa, no con una idea más. Estas son las principales: Qué no se delega. Qué decide cada persona del equipo cuando la IA propone casi todo, y quién responde de lo que produce. Un agente no es un compañero de equipo: es capacidad, y la spec pasa a ser el elemento del Product Backlog de un equipo híbrido. También, cuánto puede reducirse un equipo sin perder criterio. Acuerdos que caben en una página. Cómo se ponen de acuerdo personas y agentes: vibe coding para explorar y specs para lo que se queda, tres niveles de autonomía, y qué cambia en la Daily Scrum y en la Sprint Retrospective. Un Sprint al ritmo de la respuesta, no del código. Por qué el Sprint no se acorta solo porque construir sea rápido, cómo descubrir y entregar a la vez, y cómo planificar cuando el esfuerzo ya no es lo que limita. "Terminado" no es "el agente ha terminado". El contrato de calidad de un equipo que trabaja con IA, y qué cambia cuando el propio producto lleva IA dentro. Saber si la IA compensa. Una sola escalera de metas que une la estrategia con el Sprint, mirar el flujo de valor entero y no solo tu tramo, y medir si la IA mejora algo de verdad. Adoptar IA en la empresa con Scrum. Un backlog de casos de uso, pilotos con criterio de parada y paso a producción, con el AI Act, el RGPD y la supervisión humana dentro del backlog y de la Definición de Terminado, en vez de en un comité al final. Para quién es Para quien trabaja con Scrum: Scrum Masters, Product Owners y Product Managers, Developers, jefes de proyecto y líderes técnicos. Y, en el fondo, para cualquiera que tenga que implantar IA en su empresa con criterio y con efectividad. Doy por hecho que conoces Scrum y que ya has usado un asistente de IA. No doy por hecho que hayas trabajado con agentes, que hayas medido si la IA te mejora algo ni que conozcas el AI Act. Si lo tuyo es implantar IA en la empresa, puedes ir directo a la Parte V sin leer las anteriores. Cómo está organizado Una introducción, cinco partes y un cierre: Parte I. Lo que cambia y lo que no: cuándo Scrum ayuda y cuándo estorba, y por qué el cuello de botella siempre se mueve. Parte II. El equipo: personas y agentes: qué no se delega, el papel del Scrum Master, los agentes como capacidad, los acuerdos de trabajo, el tamaño del equipo y cómo se sigue aprendiendo cuando la IA escribe el primer borrador. Parte III. El Sprint con IA: descubrir y entregar a la vez, validar antes de construir, planificar, la duración del Sprint, los cinco eventos y la Definición de Terminado. Parte IV. items.title: Niemand bezahlt uns, um Agile zu praktizieren: Fünf Produktfragen, die stattdessen zählen 🇩🇪
items.summary: In Kürze: Fünf Produktfragen für agile Praktiker, wenn Code billig ist These : Dieser Artikel erklärt fünf Produktfragen, die an Gewicht gewinnen, wenn KI die Umsetzung von Software günstig macht, warum sinkende KI-Kosten die Menge der Arbeit erhöhen, die diese Fragen filtern müssen, und wie Teams während der frühen KI-Einführung Arbeitsprinzipien festlegen. Jahrzehntelang haben die Kosten der Softwareentwicklung rationiert, welche Produktentwicklung eine Organisation beginnen konnte: Niemand konnte es sich leisten, alles zu bauen, also musste jemand eine Auswahl treffen, wie grob auch immer. KI hat diese Rationierung nicht nur geschwächt, sondern die führenden KI-Labore sind darauf angewiesen, dass Ihre Organisation mit jeder Modellgeneration mehr KI nutzt. Hinzu kommt, dass das Produktbetriebsmodell verspricht, zu reparieren, was Agile angeblich kaputt gemacht hat. Nichts davon garantiert, dass jemand fragt, ob Ihre Arbeit ein Kundenproblem löst, und ebenso wenig, ob die Lösung die Kosten wert war. Sie müssen sich diese Produktfragen selbst beantworten. Sobald der Start neuer Arbeit wenig kostet, wird es teurer, fünf Produktfragen zu überspringen: welches Problem es wert ist, gelöst zu werden, ob die Arbeit die beste Nutzung der Zeit des Teams ist, ob sie gut genug für die Menschen ist, für die sie baut wurde, ob sie das Kundenproblem gelöst hat und ob die Arbeitsweise des Teams noch den Anforderungen genügt. KI-Agenten können die Evidenz in der ‚Assist‘-Kategorie des A3 Frameworks vorbereiten, in der Agenten analysieren und Menschen entscheiden. Explizite Standards für KI-gestützte Arbeit, etwa die AI Definition of Done, und wiederkehrende Überprüfungen, etwa der AI Delegation Audit, halten die Antworten realistisch. Ob Sie das alles Scrum nennen, ist dabei die am wenigsten interessante Frage von allen. Image Transparenzhinweis : Ich habe das Buch von Charniak und McDermott über „Artificial Intelligence“ vor Jahrzehnten gelesen; selbstverständlich nutze ich KI für Recherche, Übersetzungen, Korrekturlesen, das Hinterfragen von Spannungsbögen und Artikelstrukturen, die Erstellung von Artefakten wie Grafiken sowie für Zusammenfassungen. KI ist ein Produktionswerkzeug, kein Ersatz für das Denken. 🗞 Shall I notify you about articles like this one? Awesome! You can sign up here for the ‘Food for Agile Thought’ newsletter and join 35,000-plus subscribers . Wir werden nicht für Scrum bezahlt, wofür dann? Wenn Sie im Produktbereich arbeiten, glauben Sie vermutlich, dass die langsame, teure Entwicklung das große Problem der Softwareentwicklung war und dass KI-Coding-Agenten es endlich lösen. Die Hälfte dieser Überzeugung hält stand: Die Entwicklung war langsam und teuer, und Agenten haben das Schreiben von Code deutlich günstiger gemacht. Die andere Hälfte verdient eine genauere Prüfung, denn die Kosten erledigten eine grobe Rationierungsaufgabe, die viele Organisationen nie durch etwas Besseres ersetzt haben. Als ein neues Feature ein Team mehrere Wochen kostete, musste jemand entscheiden, welche Idee diese Wochen bekam, und manche schwache Idee starb in einem Priorisierungsmeeting, bevor jemand eine Zeile Code schrieb. (Zugegeben, es waren nicht viele; die Ideen von einem Senior-Sponsor mit Budgetbefugnis überlebten meist, und ausgewählt zu werden, sagte nichts darüber aus, ob eine Idee ein lohnendes Problem adressierte.) Dieselben Kosten richteten auch Schaden an, denn sie hielten von günstigen Experimenten ab und drängten Organisationen dazu, Features zu verteidigen, für die sie bereits bezahlt hatten. Damit lieferten sie ein Paradebeispiel für die Sunk-Cost-Falle. Das Produktmanagement hat einen Namen für die Disziplin, die die Rationierung allein nie hervorgebracht hat, und Uri Levine, Mitgründer von Waze, hat ihn 2023 zum Titel seines Buches gemacht: Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution . Wenn das Schreiben von Code so deutlich simpler wird, wird es wieder erschwinglich, sich in die eigene Lösung zu verlieben. Gleichzeitig wird es billiger denn je zu testen, ob sich Kunden für etwas interessieren. Seit Jahren beschreibe ich mit einem Satz, wofür agile Praktiker eigentlich bezahlt werden: Wir werden nicht dafür bezahlt, Scrum zu praktizieren, sondern dafür, die Probleme unserer Kunden innerhalb der gegebenen Rahmenbedingungen zu lösen und dabei zur Zukunftsfähigkeit der Organisation beizutragen. Dieser Satz – eine Umschreibung der fünf Produktfragen – scheint heute nützlicher denn je zu sein, denn Agile im Allgemeinen und Scrum im Besonderen stehen gleichzeitig von zwei Seiten unter Druck. items.title: Tokens Are Capacity, Not Value: Bringing AI Agent Cost into Sprint Planning
items.summary: Image Once a Scrum Team pays for AI agents by the token, Sprint Planning gains a question it never had: can we afford this item? In the PSM-AI and PSPO-AI classes I teach, I hear two answers to it, and both cause trouble. The first team ignores tokens. The budget is gone by day four and nobody can say where it went. The second team swings the other way and lets token cost quietly reorder the work. The cheapest items to generate go first, whatever their value. The first team runs out of money. The second runs out of value. This post describes a third way that keeps empiricism intact: treat tokens as a capacity, check them alongside the two capacities that agents put under pressure, and spend as little time estimating as possible. Where tokens belong in Sprint Planning Tokens are a capacity constraint, not a value signal. They tell the team what it can afford to do with agents this Sprint, never what is worth doing. Mapped onto the three Sprint Planning topics in the Scrum Guide: ====================================== Topic : Why is this Sprint valuable? Do tokens matter? No Topic : What can be Done this Sprint? Do tokens matter? Yes Topic : How will the chosen work get done? Do tokens matter? Yes ====================================== The Sprint Goal comes first. The token conversation starts only once the team knows what it is trying to achieve. I understand that Scrum Teams revisit their Sprint Goal based on the "What" and "How". The three-capacity check A Sprint can hold only what the tightest of three capacities allows, and with agents involved it is usually review, not tokens: Focus hours. The Developers' time after leave, holidays and Scrum events. Building, briefing agents and pairing all come from here. Token budget. The AI budget for the Sprint, after holding back a reserve (I suggest starting at 15%) for review agents, test generation and surprises. Review hours. The part of those focus hours that people who can genuinely judge agent output can spend checking it. This is not extra time, and it is usually much smaller than teams assume. This is where the core idea behind AI-augmented Scrum shows up in numbers. AI moves the constraint from generating work to verifying it. Agents add capacity to the work, but they are not team members, and accountability for what ships stays with people. A team with plenty of tokens and too little review time doesn't deliver more; it builds up verification debt faster. Start in refinement: ready before estimated The cheapest token is the one an agent never spends retrying. Vague acceptance criteria are one of the biggest drivers of token cost, because an agent with no measurable target keeps rewriting until something looks done. So the first check belongs in Product Backlog refinement, before anyone talks about cost. Two simple rules catch most of the trouble: No description or no acceptance criteria means not ready. An agent given only a title has to guess who the work is for, what done means and where to stop. Numbers, not adjectives. "Handle large files gracefully" and "should be fast" can't be tested by an agent or verified by a person. "Up to 50,000 orders download within 10 seconds" can. When I run the same feature through both versions, the vague one is estimated at about 1.1 million tokens and the refined one at about 744,000, roughly a third less, before a single line of code is written. The refined story is also far easier to review, which matters because review is usually the tightest capacity. The usual readiness signals still apply: who it is for and why, error and edge cases, what is out of scope, and whether the story is really two stories. None of this is new to Scrum Teams. Agents simply make the cost of skipping it visible. Sizing without heavy estimation You don't need a token estimate per story. A rough size per story, plus your own history, is enough. Teams I work with first tried estimating each item from scratch, with files touched, agent turns and model type, and gave up within a Sprint. Nobody has time for it. What works is the habit many teams already have: T-shirt sizes. Each size stands for typical build hours, review hours and tokens. These are just for reference. The build hours for agent items are a person's time to brief and steer the agent. The values are illustrative. Token use depends on your codebase, your agent setup and your model, and the same task can cost different amounts on different runs. So treat every figure as a range, never a commitment. This is where empiricism comes in. Tag each agent session with the Product Backlog item it served. After a couple of Sprints, record each finished item's size and the tokens it actually used, and replace the starter values with your own. The estimates stop being anyone's defaults and start reflecting your product. A worked example In this example the team worries about tokens, but review hours run out first. The team has 120 focus hours and 12 review hours. Its budget is 10 million…

items.title: You Don't Need a Transformation. You Need One Repair.
items.summary: Image You don't need a transformation. You need one repair. You've done the big change. Maybe more than once. The reorg, the new framework, the tooling migration, the all-hands where someone put "cultural change" on a slide. Months of disruption, a real budget, everybody's attention. And here you are, hitting the same frictions you started with. The status that stays green until it snaps. The retro that changes nothing. The team that waits more than it works. That isn't bad luck, and it isn't because you picked the wrong framework this time. It's because the unit of change was always too big. A transformation tries to change everything at once, which means it can't isolate what actually moved the needle, can't be inspected while it's happening, and can't be undone when a piece of it makes things worse. You find out if it worked a year later, when it's too late and too expensive to matter. There's a smaller unit that actually moves. One repair at a time. Why the big change keeps missing The gap the transformation is supposed to close is real. In Digital.ai's 2025 State of Agile, somewhere between 55 and 64% of organizations said they had good visibility into their work, while 63% in the same population said they struggled to actually deliver it. More process, more oversight, and the delivery problem is still there. That's the tell: the thing that's weak isn't the framework. It's a behavior underneath it that no rollout installs. So instead of installing another process, you repair the fundamental underneath the friction. Not all eight fundamentals, not the whole team, not this quarter. One friction, one fundamental, one small move you can watch. The loop The whole system runs on four steps. It's small enough to run this week. Spot the Friction Signal. Start from what the team actually feels, the pattern people recognize instantly. Not a complaint, not a diagnosis. "We keep getting surprised." "The real meeting happens in the hallway." Name the weak fundamental. A friction tells you where to look. A few honest questions tell you what you're looking at, the fundamental most likely under pressure. Usually more than one, which is fine. Try one Repair Move. A small, testable change you can run in a few weeks and actually inspect. Not a transformation. One thing. Observe what shifts. Then you watch, honestly. Did anything change? If nothing surfaced, the move didn't take, and that's information too. That's it. Spot, name, try, observe. Then go around again. The part that makes it honest Two things keep this from becoming just another framework. First, a friction almost never has a single cause with a single fix. The loop points you at the fundamental most likely under pressure and hands you a repair to try, not the answer. You run it as an experiment and let what shifts tell you whether you aimed right. Second, the reason a fundamental eroded almost always sits in the system around the team, not in the team's willpower. "Just be more transparent" is useless advice when roughly 6 in 10 employees say they're afraid to speak up at work, as a 2026 Radical Candor survey found. You don't fix that with a poster. You change what surfacing a problem costs, one small move at a time, and you watch whether the truth starts arriving earlier. Small enough to actually do A transformation asks you to bet a year on a change you can't inspect. A repair asks you to bet two weeks on a change you can. If it works, you feel it fast and you keep going. If it doesn't, you've lost a fortnight and learned something specific. That asymmetry is the whole argument. So the next move isn't a program. It's picking the one friction your team feels most, and the fundamental most likely under it. That takes about two minutes to find. Take the two-minute self-diagnostic → https://www.fundamentalsfirst.eu/self-diagnostic Your framework isn't broken. Your fundamentals are. Scrum on!

items.title: AI stalled: which of McKinsey's 12 operating model elements can your Scrum Team decide?
items.summary: AI work stalls when a Scrum Team acts on a decision it doesn't own, or waits on a decision nobody has delegated. The Scrum Master's job is to find out who holds that decision and get it delegated before the next Sprint. Two questions show whether the team holds a decision. First, does the Scrum Guide give it to the Scrum Team, the Developers or the Product Owner? Second, if not, has the person who holds it delegated it in writing, or in a decision the team can point to? A decision that fails both tests belongs to someone else, and the team needs that person to act. What Scrum gives the team The Scrum Guide gives the team a short list of decisions outright. The Scrum Team is self-managing, so it decides internally who does what, when and how (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). The Developers own the Sprint Backlog, which the Guide describes as a plan by and for the Developers. They also decide how to turn Product Backlog items into a usable Increment. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, and the whole organisation must respect those decisions (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). Even these decisions have a limit. When the organisation sets a Definition of Done as a standard, every Scrum Team must follow it as a minimum (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). The team decides how it works within that standard, not whether the standard applies. What McKinsey found about reinventors McKinsey's Organise to Value research describes 12 operating model elements: value agenda, structure, ecosystem, governance, processes, technology, leadership, talent, footprint, purpose, behaviours and rewards (Weddle et al., 2026). A 2026 survey of 701 senior leaders placed 415 of them in an AI maturity horizon. Of those, 53 came from organisations McKinsey calls reinventors, which redesign roles, workflows and the operating model around AI (Weddle et al., 2026). Reinventors favour decisive leaders who push decision rights down, so more choices can be made without escalation. They also favour standardised processes, with consistent workflows and clear protocols (Weddle et al., 2026). The first finding means a leader holds the authority until they delegate it to the team. The second means some decisions about how work is done stay at enterprise level by design. Standardised enterprise processes limit a decision the Scrum Guide gives to the Developers: how the work is done. The two fit together the same way a Definition of Done does: the enterprise sets the standard, and the Developers decide how to meet it. A team that rewrites an enterprise standard on its own will be overruled. A team that asks permission for a choice the Scrum Guide already gives it loses a Sprint for no reason. Who decides each of the 12 elements Each of McKinsey's 12 elements is a group of related decisions about how the organisation runs. Governance, for example, covers how priorities are set and resources allocated. Structure covers how accountable units and teams are designed (Weddle et al., 2026). In my reading of the Scrum Guide, the team makes some of the decisions in three elements and has a narrow share in two more. Leaders outside the team make every other decision unless they delegate it. Decided by the Scrum Team: some decisions in structure, processes and governance. The team organises its own work (structure). The Developers decide how to do the work, within any enterprise standards (processes). The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog (governance). Decided partly by the Scrum Team: purpose and behaviours. The Product Owner develops the Product Goal, which gives the team its purpose for the product. The Scrum values guide how the team works together (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). Leaders outside the team still decide the organisation's wider purpose and culture. Decided outside the team unless delegated: value agenda, external partners (the ecosystem element), technology, leadership, talent, footprint and rewards. The remaining decisions in structure, processes and governance are also made outside the team. These include funding, enterprise process standards and how teams are designed across the organisation. Why AI work stalls on these decisions AI work needs decisions from outside the team early. Picture a team trialling an AI coding assistant. It needs a technology decision about which tools are approved, and a decision about which data the vendor may see. It may also need a talent decision to free someone for training. None of these belongs to the team under the Scrum Guide. If the team acts anyway, the decision-maker reverses it. If the team waits without asking, the Sprint Goal slips, and that person does not know why. In my experience with Australian government agencies, technology access and funding are the two decisions that most often stall AI work. Neither is the team's failure. Both are delegations that nobody has made. How to get the decision delegated The Scrum Master serves the organisation by helping remove barriers between the Scrum…

items.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
items.summary: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely. Surprisingly, Mars may have had a better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, although even there the odds were slim. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

items.title: Leichter Rückgang bei fossilen Emissionen
items.summary: Die weltweiten CO2-Emissionen aus fossilen Brennstoffen dürften laut dem Global Carbon Project 2026 leicht zurückgehen. Ursache sei eine geringere Nutzung von Erdöl als kurzfristige Folge des Iran-Krieges. Insgesamt steige der globale Treibhausgasausstoß aber weiterhin, vor allem wegen höherer Emissionen aus Landnutzung und der Schwächung natürlicher CO2-Senken.

items.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation
items.summary: After more than a year of simulated life on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally emerged from isolation, bringing a remarkable space exploration experiment to an end. Their experiences growing food, conserving resources, and overcoming Mars-like challenges could help NASA prepare for humanity's future on the Moon and Mars.

items.title: NASA offers $500,000 to develop next-generation electric rocket engines
items.summary: NASA is putting $500,000 on the line in a new competition to accelerate the development of advanced electric rocket engines for satellites and future space exploration. The AMPERE Challenge will reward up to two U.S. companies with cash prizes and access to NASA testing facilities to help bring promising propulsion technology closer to real-world missions.

items.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

items.title: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you.

items.title: Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space
items.summary: For the first time, a robot has autonomously built part of a structure in space, demonstrating a breakthrough that could fundamentally change space exploration. The technology could one day allow scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, far beyond the size limits of today's rockets.

items.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
items.summary: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

items.title: A Painful Modernization Story
items.summary: Image Leadership at one company wanted to modernize their core platform. There was an obvious way to do it. They chose the other way. After years of investment, the modernization had delivered nothing, millions had gone to consultants, and the company was downsizing. What went wrong? The obvious way This is not a unique story. A lot of companies overcomplicate their modernizations. At this company, they already had a high-performing Scrum Team managing their core product. The obvious move was to engage their existing Product Owner and empower them to lead the modernization effort with the current Scrum Team. They already understood the business, the customers, the edge cases, and the real constraints. They had the empirical knowledge that only comes from delivering value Sprint after Sprint, and they'd just wrapped up a major initiative successfully. Done right, this was a chance to energize the team that already knew the product best. They could have started replacing the existing system a piece at a time and learning as they went. If leadership wanted to move faster, they could have added additional staff and support to the existing Scrum Team. The other way Instead of engaging their existing Scrum Team, the company formed several new Scrum Teams to do the modernization effort. Leadership then decided that because the new Scrum Teams were just rebuilding the current product, they didn't need a Product Owner . They worked for six months without a Product Owner, but nothing usable was delivered. When the organization finally did add Product Owners, they weren't really empowered to make real business decisions. It was too little, too late. Here's what went wrong: Siloed teams . Not only were they separated from the current team, but the new teams were formed around technology silos which created unnecessary dependencies. No empowered Product Owner . No one was empowered to steer the modernization effort. Big-bang thinking . Unrealistic, leadership-defined deadlines, no incremental delivery. Ignoring the people closest to the work. Money and Vice Presidents instead of engaging the team that already knew the product. No Empirical approach. They didn't adjust their delivery approach beyond just surface-level changes when things weren't going well. Development and testing were in separate Sprints. They hired a design firm who put together a front-end design and html in one Sprint, and then back-end development and testing was done in the following Sprint. Repeatedly what was delivered couldn't be used and had to be sent back which caused delays on top of delays. I have watched versions of this story play out before, and throwing more money at it is not the answer and siloed teams rarely work well. The result of getting the structure wrong Ignoring existing institutional knowledge and starting over with a group that had no empowered Product Owner was not “saving money.” It was the most expensive decision they could have made. In the end, the company wasted so much money that it led to downsizing. They never got their modernization. Instead, they got restructured. How to get it right Great modernization efforts don't happen by accident. They start with the right structure and the right people already in place. Start with good structure First off, a Product Owner is not optional. A Product Owner owns the Product Goal, orders the backlog, and makes strategic decisions. Without an empowered Product Owner, a Scrum Team is just a group of people throwing code around. Energize your high-performing teams Leadership should not redesign the org chart every time they get excited about a new technology. Leadership should remove impediments, make sure the team has the resources they need, and make sure the team is working together effectively. Keep the high-performing teams. Give them the support they need. If the old system truly needs to be replaced, the people who already understand the volume, the data, and the business rules are the ones best positioned to make that transition safely and incrementally. Plan for Incremental Delivery A year of work with nothing usable to show for it is not Agile. Modernization doesn't have to mean a big-bang rewrite. Encourage the Scrum Team to break the work down. They should deliver small, usable pieces of the new system, get feedback, and build on it. Let the team plan their own Sprints instead of chasing top-down deadlines set before anyone understood the scope of the work. Three questions to ask before you modernize If your organization is about to launch a modernization effort, ask yourself three questions. Who has organizational knowledge - Who already owns the current Product and has the deepest knowledge of it? Is the team structured for success? - Are we organizing around the Product or around technology silos? Can we allow them to self-organize? Are we planning for incremental delivery? - Will we deliver usable increments every Sprint, or are we planning a multi-year rewrite…

items.title: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
items.summary: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations. Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

items.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
items.summary: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

items.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
items.summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

items.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
items.summary: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

items.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
items.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

items.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.
